paragraphs: Nesterov’s accelerated gradient method is an optimization procedure whose behavior can be studied through a continuous dynamical system. This paper develops that perspective without relying on the argument that the optimization step size must shrink toward zero. It therefore provides a different route for connecting an iterative algorithm to an underlying differential equation.

The authors show that Nesterov acceleration arises when an ordinary differential equation is discretized using a semi-implicit Euler scheme. Discretization converts continuous evolution into a sequence of updates. The integration scheme matters here: the connection identifies how the continuous system and the particular update procedure fit together, rather than merely treating them as loosely similar descriptions.

By analyzing both descriptions, the paper investigates what produces acceleration and establishes further connections between their dynamics. The analysis suggests that damping dependent on curvature is central to the effect. That is an explanatory conclusion supported by the analysis, rather than a universal assertion that every accelerated method must operate through precisely the same mechanism.
icml-2019-a-dynamical-systems-perspectiv.tldr: A differential-equation view of Nesterov acceleration suggests that curvature-dependent damping helps explain its behavior.

paragraphs: This paper studies high-dimensional Bayesian optimization through searches in lower-dimensional embedded spaces. The relevant idea is that an optimization problem may have an unknown low-dimensional active subspace. An embedding offers a way to conduct the search in fewer dimensions, but its usefulness depends on how faithfully it preserves the model needed for optimization.

The authors establish a tight bound on the error introduced into the Gaussian process model by moving from the original domain to the embedding. Their result implies that optimization in the embedded space proceeds essentially as though it had direct access to the unknown active subspace. The argument covers a broad class of algorithms and Gaussian process models, including models with non-stationary kernels.

The paper also supplies an efficient implementation using hashing. In the reported experiments, its embedding produces considerably better results than earlier approaches based on Gaussian matrix projections and structure learning. The contribution combines a theoretical justification for reducing the search dimension with an implementation whose empirical performance supports that approach.
icml-2019-a-framework-for-bayesian-optim.tldr: Low-dimensional embeddings enable Bayesian optimization with bounded Gaussian process error and strong reported empirical performance.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic space is useful for representing data with hierarchical structure, but probabilistic learning also requires distributions that can be evaluated and optimized in that geometry. This paper introduces a wrapped normal distribution on hyperbolic space to supply those computational ingredients. Its contribution concerns both the geometry of representations and the tractability of learning probability models over them.

The proposed distribution has a density that can be evaluated analytically and differentiated with respect to its parameters. These properties make it suitable for gradient-based learning. The authors also provide sampling without auxiliary procedures such as rejection sampling. Together, evaluation, differentiation, and sampling give probabilistic models practical ways to use the hyperbolic distribution during learning.

The paper develops two applications: a hyperbolic version of a variational autoencoder and probabilistic word embeddings in hyperbolic space. It demonstrates the distribution’s effectiveness on datasets including MNIST, Atari 2600 Breakout, and WordNet. These applications show how the same distribution can support different learning tasks while retaining the geometry intended to represent hierarchical relationships.
icml-2019-a-wrapped-normal-distribution-.tldr: A tractable wrapped normal distribution makes gradient-based probabilistic learning possible in hyperbolic space.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains a shared model from data supplied by many clients. The paper argues that existing training and inference practices can favor some clients over others. It proposes an objective designed for target populations formed by mixtures of client distributions, so the model is not optimized solely around one particular balance of clients.

This agnostic formulation also produces a notion of fairness tied to performance across those mixtures. The authors provide data-dependent learning guarantees using Rademacher complexity, a measure used to relate a model class to its ability to fit data. These guarantees help guide the learning algorithm, connecting the proposed objective to an analysis of generalization.

The paper additionally develops a fast stochastic optimization algorithm and proves convergence bounds when both the loss and the hypothesis set are convex. Experiments on several datasets demonstrate benefits of the approach. Its broader relevance is to situations where training and deployment distributions differ: the mixture-based formulation offers a way to account for uncertainty about which populations a shared model will serve.
icml-2019-agnostic-federated-learning-d4.tldr: Agnostic federated learning optimizes a shared model across mixtures of client populations, linking distributional robustness with fairness.

paragraphs: The paper addresses anomaly detection when training data describes normal cases but cannot represent the full variety of possible anomalies. In this one-class setting, a model must learn what belongs to the normal population. The authors focus on making that learning more efficient for high-dimensional inputs such as images, where modeling the input distribution can be difficult.

Their method uses a multi-hypotheses autoencoder to learn the normal-data distribution. A discriminator critiques the model with two complementary purposes: discouraging artificial modes unsupported by the data and encouraging diversity among hypotheses. Multiple hypotheses therefore provide different possibilities, while the discriminator helps keep those possibilities grounded in the observed normal cases.

The resulting framework identifies samples outside the learned distribution. On CIFAR-10, the paper reports improvements of up to 3.9 percentage points over previously reported anomaly-detection results. On a real anomaly-detection task, it reduces baseline error from 6.8% to 1.5%. These findings support the proposed combination of diverse predictions and discriminator feedback in the evaluated settings.
icml-2019-anomaly-detection-with-multipl.tldr: A multi-hypotheses autoencoder with discriminator feedback improves anomaly detection by learning diverse, data-supported normal patterns.

paragraphs: Dropout helps prevent overfitting, but explaining why it works has motivated several different interpretations. This paper places dropout inside a broader framework for multiplicative noise in neural networks. It treats both Bernoulli noise, which corresponds to dropout, and continuous noise distributions, connecting these training procedures to probabilistic assumptions about network weights.

The authors show that multiplicative noise induces structured shrinkage priors: priors that encourage weights to shrink in a coordinated way. They derive this equivalence exactly through reparameterization properties of scale mixtures. A separate result concerns the training objective: dropout’s Monte Carlo objective approximates marginal maximum a posteriori estimation. The exact equivalence and the approximate estimation interpretation are distinct claims.

Using this connection, the paper introduces a shrinkage framework for residual networks called automatic depth determination. It extends the idea of automatically determining relevance to network depth. The authors also investigate two inference strategies that improve on the stated maximum a posteriori approximation in regression benchmarks, turning the interpretation into concrete alternatives for learning.
icml-2019-dropout-as-a-structured-shrink.tldr: An exact connection between multiplicative noise and shrinkage priors explains dropout and motivates new residual-network inference methods.

paragraphs: This paper changes the mathematical object used to describe data for generative modeling. Instead of representing samples only through a probability distribution, it uses currents, which generalize oriented geometric surfaces. Probability distributions correspond to the zero-dimensional case. Higher-dimensional currents let the representation attach an oriented tangent plane to each sample, explicitly recording local geometric direction.

The authors build FlatGAN using the flat metric, a distance between currents. This gives a formulation in the spirit of generative adversarial networks while allowing the training objects to include orientation. They also prove that the flat distance between a parameterized current and a reference current is Lipschitz continuous in the parameters, providing a regularity result for how that distance changes.

Experiments show that moving beyond zero-dimensional currents produces interpretable, disentangled latent representations. Those representations behave equivariantly with respect to the specified tangent planes: their behavior changes in a corresponding way with the supplied orientations. The findings suggest that explicitly incorporating local geometric information can shape the organization of learned latent representations.
icml-2019-flat-metric-minimization-with-.tldr: FlatGAN models oriented geometric data using currents, yielding interpretable latent representations in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper combines a predictive model with a generative model in one neural architecture. A deep invertible transformation, or normalizing flow, computes features, and a linear model makes predictions from them. The aim is to retain useful predictive accuracy while also modeling the feature distribution, giving the system more probabilistic information than predictions alone.

A central property is that a single feed-forward pass computes both the feature density and the conditional distribution of targets given features exactly. These quantities also provide the exact joint density of targets and features. Their availability makes it straightforward to compute additional probabilistic quantities needed by downstream applications.

The authors report accuracy similar to purely predictive models despite the invertibility requirement. They also find that the generative component remains a good model of the input features under the combined training objective. This supports capabilities such as detecting out-of-distribution inputs and learning with partially labeled data. The contribution is a tractable shared architecture whose predictive and generative roles remain useful together.
icml-2019-hybrid-models-with-deep-and-in.tldr: An invertible feature model combines competitive prediction with exact density evaluation in a single forward pass.

paragraphs: Multi-label classification assigns several labels to the same example, so relationships among labels can be useful for prediction. Classifier chains exploit those relationships by predicting labels in sequence. The paper questions the use of one fixed sequence for every context and proposes choosing the label ordering dynamically as part of the prediction approach.

The method has two components. A simple algorithm resembling expectation-maximization bootstraps the learned model, while a more elaborate reinforcement-learning approach learns context-dependent ordering. This makes the sequence itself part of the learning problem. The intended benefit is to exploit label dependencies explicitly without requiring the same order to work equally well for all contexts.

On three public benchmarks, the reinforcement-learning version outperforms recurrent neural networks that use fixed label orderings. The improvements occur on all three datasets for both bipartition measures, which assess label decisions, and ranking measures, which assess label ordering quality. These results support dynamic ordering as a useful ingredient in sequence-based multi-label classification within the evaluated settings.
icml-2019-learning-context-dependent-lab.tldr: Learning context-dependent label orderings improves sequence-based multi-label classification over fixed-order recurrent models on three benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper studies decision policies learned from data that may reflect existing discrimination. Bias can enter through data collection, variable definitions, and the translation of findings into decisions. The authors therefore consider fairness in both the decisions a policy makes and the outcomes those decisions help produce, focusing on unfair dependence on sensitive attributes.

Their approach combines causal inference with constrained optimization. Causal reasoning addresses how sensitive features relate to decisions and outcomes, while optimization seeks a policy that performs well subject to specified fairness requirements. This formulation treats fairness as a restriction on the policy-learning problem and is designed to address multiple potential sources of bias.

The proposed method comes with a theoretical guarantee that the selected fair policy induces a joint distribution for new instances satisfying the given fairness constraints. That guarantee concerns the specified constraints, rather than every possible meaning of fairness. Illustrations using synthetic and real criminal justice data show how the framework can be applied to consequential decision settings.
icml-2019-learning-optimal-fair-policies.tldr: Causal inference and constrained optimization produce policies with guarantees for specified fairness constraints on future instances.

paragraphs: This paper examines how a bidder should act when an auction seller sets reserve prices using bid distributions. In these prior-dependent, revenue-maximizing auctions, the distribution of submitted bids is part of the seller’s pricing procedure. The study considers a setting with one strategic bidder and asks how that bidder can optimize a bidding strategy.

The authors use a variational approach to analyze the original objective, treating the bidding strategy as the object being optimized. They then introduce a relaxed objective that can be handled with gradient descent. The relaxation supplies a practical route for searching over strategies when directly working with the original objective is difficult.

The approach is presented as general enough to accommodate various value distributions and revenue-maximizing mechanisms. The derived strategies deliver very large gains compared with truthful bidding in the study. This finding concerns the specified setting in which reserve prices depend on bid distributions and one bidder behaves strategically. It highlights the value of optimizing behavior with the seller’s pricing rule explicitly in view.
icml-2019-learning-to-bid-in-revenue-max.tldr: A relaxed optimization objective enables bidding strategies that substantially outperform truthful bidding in the studied reserve-price setting.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how regularization and optimization can favor particular solutions in deep models. Its focus is margin maximization and its connection to complexity control. The analysis covers both homogeneous and non-homogeneous models, extending earlier work that examined infinitesimal regularization only for homogeneous models.

The authors study a constrained path: the limiting behavior of loss minimization as the allowed parameter norm grows without bound. They connect this path to a margin-based path and characterize the selected solution. For non-homogeneous ensembles formed by adding homogeneous sub-models, the limiting solution discards the shallowest sub-models when they are unnecessary. This gives a depth-sensitive description of the preference induced by the optimization formulation.

For homogeneous models, the paper establishes convergence to a lexicographic maximum-margin solution, which refines how margin solutions are selected. It also gives conditions under which unconstrained gradient descent reaches maximum-margin solutions in the limit. The gradient-descent conclusion is conditional, while the overall analysis clarifies how model structure affects the solutions selected by limiting optimization procedures.
icml-2019-lexicographic-and-depth-sensit.tldr: Limiting optimization paths reveal margin-based solution preferences that depend on model homogeneity and depth.

paragraphs: The paper starts from the idea that efficiency requirements can influence the design of a learning loss itself. It introduces Q-loss, a strictly proper, canonical, twice-differentiable loss. Its mirror update can operate on arbitrary rational inputs using integer arithmetic with addition, subtraction, division, multiplication, and absolute value, connecting the mathematical objective to computational requirements.

Building on Q-loss, the authors construct a training algorithm that retains boosting guarantees without loss under mild assumptions. They also identify conditions under which its weights can be quantized while preserving those guarantees. Since weights are the algorithm’s main memory cost, this directly addresses storage demands while specifying when the theoretical boosting properties remain intact.

Experiments show that the method can converge quickly during early boosting rounds compared with AdaBoost, even when weight storage is more than thirty times smaller. The paper additionally uses the Bayes risk of Q-loss as a decision-tree splitting criterion and establishes optimal boosting convergence for that construction. The findings connect loss design, compact computation, and boosting theory.
icml-2019-lossless-or-quantized-boosting.tldr: Q-loss supports integer-arithmetic boosting and conditional weight quantization while retaining boosting guarantees.

paragraphs: Langevin Monte Carlo resembles gradient descent with added Gaussian noise. Fractional Langevin Monte Carlo replaces that noise with a heavy-tailed alpha-stable distribution, allowing occasional large jumps. Earlier empirical work had suggested advantages for optimization and sampling, but the available convergence theory for the fractional method described only its asymptotic behavior.

This paper analyzes what happens within finite time when the fractional method is used for non-convex optimization. The authors prove bounds on expected suboptimality, giving a theoretical description of how far the method’s result can remain from the optimum. This fills the gap between eventual convergence statements and guarantees relevant to a finite run of the algorithm.

The analysis finds that the fractional method’s weak error increases faster than that of ordinary Langevin Monte Carlo, suggesting the use of smaller step sizes. The authors also extend the results to stochastic gradients in place of exact gradients and obtain similar conclusions. The contribution therefore clarifies both finite-time behavior and a step-size implication of using heavy-tailed perturbations.
icml-2019-non-asymptotic-analysis-of-fra.tldr: Finite-time bounds for fractional Langevin optimization suggest smaller step sizes than for its Gaussian-noise counterpart.

paragraphs: This paper examines the geometry of neural-network loss functions through their sublevel sets. A sublevel set collects all parameter choices whose loss is at or below a selected threshold. Studying these sets asks whether solutions with sufficiently low loss occupy one connected region or separate regions divided by higher-loss territory.

For a class of deep, over-parameterized networks with piecewise linear activation functions, the paper proves that every sublevel set is connected and unbounded. Connectedness rules out disconnected regions at a given loss threshold. Unboundedness describes a different feature: these regions are not confined to a bounded portion of parameter space. Both properties concern the loss landscape of the network class covered by the result.

The authors conclude that this landscape has no bad local valleys and that all global minima belong to a single connected global valley, which may be very large. The result gives a structural explanation of how optimal solutions relate to one another. Its scope is the stated network class, rather than deep learning architectures in general.
icml-2019-on-connected-sublevel-sets-in-.tldr: A class of over-parameterized, piecewise-linear networks has connected, unbounded loss sublevel sets and one connected global valley.

paragraphs: Sparse networks can be trained by changing which parameters are nonzero throughout learning, avoiding the need to first train a large dense model. This paper introduces a dynamic sparse reparameterization method that addresses computational cost and the manual allocation of free parameters across layers. It treats the arrangement of the available parameters as something training can continually explore.

In evaluations on deep convolutional networks, the method achieves better accuracy for a fixed parameter budget than the compared static and dynamic reparameterization methods. Its accuracy is also on par with models obtained by iteratively pruning a pretrained dense network. These results support direct sparse training as an effective use of a limited parameter budget.

The authors investigate why the resulting networks generalize well. Neither the final sparse structure nor the initialization of its nonzero parameters sufficiently explains the observed advantage. Instead, effective learning depends crucially on continued exploration of sparse structures during training. The work therefore suggests that structural flexibility during learning can be more effective than simply adding parameters.
icml-2019-parameter-efficient-training-o.tldr: Continually reallocating sparse parameters improves accuracy under a fixed budget, with ongoing structural exploration driving the reported gains.

paragraphs: The paper studies adversarial examples when an attacker can query a classifier but cannot directly access its gradients. Gradient-based attacks can be effective when that information is available. In the black-box setting, estimating gradients through queries introduces a substantial cost, making the number of model queries a central practical concern.

The authors replace the original optimization problem with an efficient discrete surrogate. This changes the search procedure so that it does not need to estimate the gradient. As a consequence, it also avoids tuning the hyperparameters associated with first-order updates. The method’s contribution is therefore a different optimization formulation for finding adversarial examples under query-only access.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet report state-of-the-art black-box attack performance together with a significant reduction in required queries relative to several recently proposed methods. These findings support the discrete formulation as a query-efficient alternative in the tested settings. The reported gains concern both the effectiveness of the attack and the amount of classifier access needed to carry it out.
icml-2019-parsimonious-black-box-adversa.tldr: A discrete optimization surrogate produces effective black-box adversarial attacks with fewer queries and no gradient estimation.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovery of a low-rank matrix when each column is observed only through magnitudes of linear projections. The missing phase information makes these measurements incomplete in a particular way. The low-rank structure supplies a relationship among columns that the proposed algorithms can use, with applications including dynamic imaging of live biological specimens.

For this recovery problem, the authors provide simple algorithms with theoretical guarantees. In the small-rank regime, the required sample complexity is only slightly above the order-optimal amount and substantially below the requirements of standard phase-retrieval methods that do not exploit the shared structure. The gain comes from treating the columns as a related low-rank collection.

The paper also considers a dynamic version in which the low-dimensional subspace generating the signals can change over time. It introduces an algorithm with a correctness guarantee when those changes are piecewise constant. This extends the recovery framework to changing signal collections while making the temporal assumption behind the guarantee explicit.
icml-2019-phaseless-pca-low-rank-matrix-.tldr: Provable algorithms exploit low-rank structure to recover signals from magnitude-only measurements, including piecewise-constant subspace changes.

paragraphs: Relational Pooling is a framework for representing graphs that extends beyond approaches built around the Weisfeiler-Lehman algorithm, graph Laplacians, or diffusion. The paper derives the framework from finite partial exchangeability and describes it as having maximal representation power for graphs. Its central concern is how much information a graph representation can distinguish and retain.

The framework can incorporate existing graph representation models and increase their expressive power. In particular, the authors show that it can make such models more powerful than the original Weisfeiler-Lehman isomorphism test. Relational Pooling also provides a theoretically sound way to use recurrent and convolutional neural networks for graph classification, broadening the range of architectures available for the task.

The authors report improved performance over state-of-the-art methods across several tasks. These experiments complement the expressiveness argument: the framework offers both a theoretical expansion of representational capability and observed benefits in evaluated applications. Its importance lies in treating graph representation as a general framework that can strengthen existing models and accommodate other neural architectures.
icml-2019-relational-pooling-for-graph-r.tldr: Relational Pooling expands graph representation power and enables existing neural architectures to support principled graph classification.

paragraphs: Experience replay improves data efficiency by reusing past interactions to update a reinforcement-learning policy. However, those interactions may become less suitable as the current policy moves away from the behavior that generated them. This paper addresses the resulting deterioration in update accuracy by actively managing the relationship between the policy and replayed experience.

Remember and Forget Experience Replay uses two mechanisms. It skips gradients from experiences that are too unlikely under the current policy, and it constrains policy changes within a trust region of replayed behaviors. The first mechanism filters unsuitable updates; the second regulates how far learning moves away from the experience being reused.

The authors combine the method with Q-learning, deterministic policy gradients, and off-policy gradient methods. They find consistent improvements for continuous-action, off-policy learning on fully observable benchmarks and partially observable flow-control problems. These results support controlling policy–experience compatibility as a useful way to improve replay. The method addresses both which past experiences contribute gradients and how rapidly the policy changes.
icml-2019-remember-and-forget-for-experi.tldr: ReF-ER improves experience replay by filtering unlikely past experiences and keeping policy changes close to replayed behaviors.

paragraphs: Bayesian probabilistic PCA and related factor models can have multiple parameter descriptions with the same likelihood because rotating the factors leaves the model unchanged. This symmetry creates continuous regions of equal posterior density. It complicates inference and makes averages of factor loadings meaningless even though the model’s predictions remain unambiguous.

The paper proposes a parameterization based on Householder transformations that removes this rotational symmetry from the posterior. The authors also use random matrix theory to establish the parameter distribution needed to preserve the original model. This preservation matters because changing how parameters are represented should not inadvertently change the probabilistic model being fitted.

Their construction avoids computing the Jacobian determinant of the parameter transformation, simplifying implementation. The authors implement the model in Stan and illustrate it with several examples. The contribution addresses a source of ambiguity in Bayesian factor models while retaining their original probabilistic meaning, allowing inference and interpretation to work with a representation that no longer contains the same rotational redundancy.
icml-2019-rotation-invariant-householder.tldr: A Householder-based parameterization removes rotational ambiguity in Bayesian PCA while preserving the original probabilistic model.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to tune regularization parameters while controlling the accuracy of the search. It develops a unified framework for approximating the regularization path, the collection of solutions obtained as regularization varies, within a prescribed tolerance. This makes the desired approximation accuracy an explicit part of the tuning procedure.

The authors establish complexity of O(epsilon^(-1/d)) for uniformly convex losses of order d at least two, and O(epsilon^(-1/2)) for generalized self-concordant functions. The framework includes least-squares and logistic regression. These results connect the amount of work needed to the requested tolerance and the mathematical properties of the loss function.

The technique also yields refined validation-error bounds and a practical hyperparameter-tuning algorithm with a global convergence guarantee for a prescribed validation-set accuracy. It automatically calibrates the stopping criterion for training optimization from that target. This connects two decisions that practitioners otherwise have to make separately: how accurately to solve each training problem and how accurately to tune the regularization parameter.
icml-2019-safe-grid-search-with-optimal-.tldr: A tolerance-controlled regularization search provides complexity guarantees and automatically sets training stopping criteria from validation accuracy targets.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent without replacement avoids independently redrawing samples during a pass through the data. It often performs better in practice than sampling with replacement, but analyzing it is difficult because the iterates and gradients become dependent. This paper tackles that dependence to obtain finite-time convergence results for general smooth, strongly convex objectives.

The authors use exchangeable pairs to bound Wasserstein distance and analyze the coupled quantities. For a sufficiently large number K of passes over the data, they establish an O(1/K²) convergence rate, compared with the known O(1/K) rate for ordinary SGD. Their analysis does not require the additional Hessian Lipschitz assumption used in earlier results for this setting.

For smaller K, the paper shows that sampling without replacement can match SGD’s rate for general smooth, strongly convex functions. It also improves dependence on problem parameters such as the condition number in both regimes. The findings distinguish the advantage available after sufficiently many passes from the matching guarantee established for shorter runs.
icml-2019-sgd-without-replacement-sharpe.tldr: For smooth, strongly convex objectives, SGD without replacement achieves sharper convergence rates when enough data passes are made.

paragraphs: Standard supervised neural-network training uses an output loss whose gradient is propagated back through hidden layers. This paper instead studies layer-wise training, where hidden layers receive locally generated error signals. The central question is whether these local objectives can support strong image-classification performance without relying on a single global error to direct every hidden-layer update.

The authors use single-layer subnetworks and two supervised loss functions to generate the local signals. They show that combining the losses helps optimization in the local-learning setting. Across a variety of image datasets, their layer-wise approach can approach state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating that local objectives can provide useful training guidance throughout a network.

The paper also considers biological plausibility, since local errors avoid transporting the global error back to hidden layers. It presents this as a possible step toward more biologically plausible learning. A completely backpropagation-free variant outperforms previously reported results among methods pursuing that aim. This variant is a separate result from the broader finding about the competitiveness of layer-wise training.
icml-2019-training-neural-networks-with-.tldr: Combining local supervised losses lets layer-wise neural-network training approach state-of-the-art image-classification performance.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers learning from a large teacher model to a smaller student. Conventional approaches use the teacher’s training data or metadata extracted from it, but access to those resources may be impractical because of dataset size or privacy and safety concerns. This paper proposes distillation without either the original data or its metadata.

The method synthesizes Data Impressions from the trained teacher and uses them as substitutes for training examples. These synthetic inputs provide the material through which the student learns from the teacher. The key shift is to derive the transfer data from the model itself, allowing the distillation process to proceed when the original dataset is unavailable.

Across multiple benchmark datasets, the authors report generalization performance competitive with distillation that uses actual training samples. This supports the feasibility of transferring useful behavior through teacher-generated surrogate data in the evaluated settings. The zero-shot designation refers to dispensing with the original training data and metadata; the trained teacher remains the source from which the impressions and transferred learning are obtained.
icml-2019-zero-shot-knowledge-distillati.tldr: Teacher-generated synthetic Data Impressions enable competitive knowledge distillation without original training data or metadata.
